develop a clinical practice guideline (CPG) synthesizing the evidence for physical therapy management of fall risk in communitydwelling older adults. The GDG consisted of five physical therapists with clinical expertise in the management of fall risk in older
adults and methodological expertise in evidence-based document development. The CPG includes a systematic review of
existing literature, and stringent methodology developed by the
American Physical Therapy Association to form the evidencebased recommendations. The CPG content, including methodology, recommendations and algorithm were externally
reviewed by clinical providers and academicians with expertise in
fall risk management for older adults. These recommendations
are intended to assist physical therapists and physical therapist
assistants who are engaged in fall risk management for
community-dwelling older adults.
Key Words: fall risk, guidelines, older adults

(J Geriatr Phys Ther 2025;48(2):62-87.)

CLINICAL IMPLICATIONS
• Physical therapists can use the evidence-based algorithm to facilitate clinical reasoning in the management
of fall risk for older adults.
• Multicomponent exercise is the most important intervention for addressing falls and fall risk in older adults.
• Multicomponent exercise must include progressive and
challenging balance training exercises and may include
other types of exercise.

SUMMARY OF GRADED RECOMMENDATIONS
This clinical practice guideline (CPG) provides recommendations for the management of fall risk in communitydwelling adults aged 65 and over (subsequently referred
to as older adult(s)). Multifactorial management programs
include screening, assessment, referral to appropriate providers, and interventions within physical therapist (PT) and
physical therapist assistant (PTA) scope of practice. This
guideline strongly recommends that PTs and PTAs

chunks.text:
participate in multifactorial management programs
addressing falls and fall risk for older adults. A multifactorial approach to fall risk management in older
adults is supported by robust evidence (Evidence
Quality/Level: I, Recommendation Strength: Strong).
A multicomponent exercise program that incorporates
balance training and other modes of exercise, such as
resistance training or Tai Chi, is strongly recommended
for reducing the risk and rate of falls (Evidence Quality/
Level: I, Recommendation Strength: Strong). The guideline
strongly recommends that balance training interventions
be progressive and sufficiently challenging, involve limb
and whole-body movements, changes in base of support,
and reduced upper limb support (Evidence Quality/Level: I,
Recommendation Strength: Strong). Additionally, Tai Chi
is strongly recommended for older adults in particular
those at lower fall risk (Evidence Quality/Level: I,
Recommendation Strength: Strong). The guideline makes
a strong recommendation for environmental assessments
and necessary modifications for older adults at higher risk
(Evidence Quality/Level: I, Recommendation Strength:
Strong). Providing or prescribing resistance training
ALONE to reduce fall risk and rate is not recommended,
as it offers limited benefits.(Evidence Quality/Level: II,
Recommendation Strength: Moderate).

This guideline also provides several weak recommendations. While reactive step (perturbation) training is
a potential component of balance training, the evidence
supporting this intervention is mixed (Evidence Quality/
Level: II, Recommendation Strength: Weak) in comparison to strong evidence for volitional step training or balance training. Additionally, this guideline recommends
a comprehensive approach that combines tailored education with individualized exercise intervention, addressing
identified risk factors, home hazards, strength and balance impairments, and referral to other providers when
necessary, especially for factors outside the scope of physical therapy (Evidence Quality/Level: V, Recommendation
Strength: Expert Opinion). The recommendation for this
comprehensive approach is predicated upon expert opinion, but each individual component is recommended
based upon robust evidence. These recommendations collectively guide physical therapists in adopting evidencebased practices to manage fall risk, while also highlighting
the limitations and areas requiring further research.

chunks.text:
Overview
Falls among older adults are a major problem for individuals, their social networks, and society. The risk of falls
increases with age. Falls often result in serious consequences including fall-related injuries, loss of function
and independence, hospitalization, institutionalization,
and death. Multiple risk factors and evidence-based interventions have been identified, some of which fall within
the scope of physical therapist and physical therapist

assistant practice. Physical therapists and physical therapist assistants enable patients to maintain, restore, and
improve movement, activity, and function to optimize
performance and enhance health, well-being, and quality
of life. Therefore, the development of guidance documents to support the implementation of evidence-based
approaches is warranted.

Burden
Falls are a major health concern in the United States and
globally that results in significant economic and health
burden. A fall is defined by The Prevention of Falls
Network (ProFaNE) group and the Center for Medicare
and Medicaid Services (CMS) as an unexpected or unintentional event in which the participants come to rest on
the ground, floor or lower level.1,2 Falls are common in
the United States, where data from the 2020 Behavioral
Risk Factor Surveillance System demonstrated 27.6% of
older adults reporting one fall in the past year (more than
14 million total falls) resulting in almost 39 000 fallrelated deaths.3 The age-adjusted death rate due to a fall
was 78 per 100 000, and has been increasing over the
last 10 years.3 Falls contribute to substantial morbidity,
health care utilization, and medical expenditures, with the
cost of fatal and non-fatal falls exceeding $50 billion
per year in the United States,4 and the cost of falls is
expected to reach $100 billion annually by 2030.5

Worldwide, falls are the second leading cause of unintentional injury deaths, with an estimated 684 000 fall deaths
per year.6 The substantial impact falls have upon older
adults supports the need for evidence-based clinical
guidance.

Etiology and Risk Factors
Falls result from multiple causes including the individual’s
environmental and social context and the situation surrounding a fall event. Aging adults experience changes in
all major bodily systems that impact physical health,7

mental health,8 and their ability to interact with their
environment.9 Almost half of falls in older adults have
been attributed to modifiable factors such as environmental factors or impairments in balance and walking.10

Certain predisposing risk factors have also been identified
including older age, a previous fall, depression, dementia,
comorbidities, psychotropic medications, and footwear.11

table_rows:
Physical therapists should participate in multifactoriala management programs addressing falls and
fall risk for older adults.

Physical therapists must provide or prescribe multicomponentb exercise to older adults to reduce
risk and rate of falls and it must include balance training and may include other exercise modes.

Physical therapists must prescribe exercise programs to older adults to be performed at least
150 minutes to 3 hours per week, lasting from 6 to 12 months, and must include progressive and
suffciiently challenging balance training.

Physical therapists must provide or prescribe balance training to older adults that is progressive
and sufficiently challenging as evidenced by movement of the limbs and whole body in multiple
directions, changing the base of support, and reducing upper limb support either alone or as part
of a multicomponent program to reduce the risk and rate of falls.
Balance training must include volitional step training and/or gait adaptability training.
Balance training may also include reactive step (perturbation) training.

Physical therapists should NOT provide or prescribe resistance training ALONE to older adults if the
purpose is to reduce the risk and/or rate of falls.
Physical therapists should prescribe Tai Chi for older adults to reduce the risk and rate of falls.

Physical therapists should NOT provide education ALONE to older adults to reduce the risk and/or
rate of falls.

Physical therapists should provide tailored education combined with individualized exercise
intervention to older adults. The tailored education should include specific actions to address
identified risk factors, including home hazards and strength and balance impairments, and
should also include referral to appropriate providers for risk factors outside of PT scope of
practice.

Physical therapists should provide environmental assessment and recommend modifications to
older adults at high risk of falls.

aMultifactorial management includes screening, assessment, referral to appropriate provider, and interventions within physical therapist scope of practice.
bMulticomponent exercise refers to exercise that includes more than one category of exercise according to the PROFANE1 taxonomy (balance and functional, felxibility, resistance training, 3-D).

These documents lacked specificity to comprehensively
guide physical therapy management of falls and fall risk
in older adults. The present CPG fills this gap by conducting a review of the primary literature on physical therapist
fall risk management, with particular attention to dosage
(ie, sets, repetitions, load), modes of delivery (type of
exercise), and the influence of physical function on levels
of fall risk. This CPG provides recommendations (see
Table 1 for summary of recommendations), a decision
algorithm to facilitate implementation of the recommendations (Figure 1), discusses limitations in the literature,
gaps in evidence, areas that require future research, and
potential benefits and risks to implementing each recommendation when information was available.

Intended Users
This CPG is intended to be used by physical therapists,
and physical therapist assistants under the supervision of
physical therapists, for the management of falls and fall
risk in community-dwelling older adults. Given the multifactorial nature of falls, a variety of health care providers
will benefit from the recommendations provided in this

Multicomponent Exercise Dosage: Provided in group or individual delivery format, for at least 3 hours/week and total volume > 50 hours
over 6-12 months. Must include balance training component.
Balance Training Dosage: Progressively reduce the BOS, movement of the body within and beyond the BOS through reaching, voluntary
stepping to adapt gait and prevent falling, and reactive stepping in response to an external perturbation to balance, reduce reliance on
upper limb support, 3+ hours/week and total volume of >50 hours.
Tai Chi Dosage: Provided 3+ times/week for a total volume of 30-60 hours.

This document is intended to guide primarily physical
therapists and physical therapist assistants in the management of fall risk in older adults. Secondarily, this CPG
may provide guidance to older adults, family members,
educators, researchers, policymakers, and payers. It is not
intended to be construed or to serve as a legal standard of
care or as an insurance benefit determination document.
As rehabilitation knowledge expands, CPGs are promoted as syntheses of current research and provisional
proposals of recommended actions under specific conditions. Standards of care are determined based on all clinical data available for an individual patient/client and are
subject to change as knowledge and technology advance,
patterns of care evolve, and patient/family values are integrated. This CPG is a summary of practice recommendations that are supported by current published literature
that has been reviewed by expert practitioners and other
interested parties. These parameters of practice should be
considered guidelines only, not mandates. Adherence to
them will not ensure a successful outcome for every
patient, nor should they be construed as including all
proper methods of care or excluding other acceptable
methods of care aimed at the same results.

This CPG includes interventions provided in group settings and in individual one on one clinical settings. Some
older adults can exercise without supervision in group
settings, while others may need one-on-one intervention
to safely exercise. Individualized exercise prescription
should be driven by a targeted PT examination and evaluation of the movement system to identify impairments that
contribute to the risk identified with performance based
and self-report measures. Recommendations for specific
examination tests and measures to support individualized
exercise prescription are outside the scope of this CPG.

published guidance statement12 to inform recommendations on screening and examination. Intervention recommendations were formed from a comprehensive review
of the literature performed by the GDG on physical
therapist interventions.

The GDG collaborated with a research librarian
with expertise in SR processes to develop the search strategies. The search strategies and results are provided in
Supplemental Digital Content, Appendices I (http://links.
lww.com/JGPT/A267) and II. The inclusion criteria were:

• publication time frame: Studies published between
2005 and 2022 were included.
• design: SRs and meta-analyses were included.
• population: Studies of community-dwelling older
adults with a mean age greater than or equal to
65 years or older were included. Studies that
included individuals with mild cognitive impairment
were included.
• interventions: Studies of interventions within the
scope of PT practice including exercise, mobility
training, balance training, education, environmental
modification, and footwear were included. All comparators were included, because a priori we intended
to determine the influence of physical function on
intervention effectiveness.
• outcomes: Studies that reported falls as number,
rate, or risk, whether injurious or not, regardless
of whether medical attention was required were
included. Rate ratio refers to the relative difference
in the fall rate (number of falls) between the intervention and comparator groups. Risk ratio refers to
the relative difference in the fall risk (number of
fallers) between the intervention and comparator
groups.

Exclusion criteria were:

• Studies focused on individuals with specific conditions, such as hip fracture, osteoporosis, Parkinson’s
disease, and dementia including moderate and severe
cognitive impairment were excluded.

Article Screening, Review, and Critical Appraisal
Process
Title and abstract screening and full-text eligibility reviews
were conducted by two independent GDG members using
the pre-specified inclusion and exclusion criteria described
above. Discrepancies were discussed by the two reviewers,
and if consensus was not reached, a third reviewer was
enlisted. Two members of the GDG independently assigned
each included study a level of evidence based upon study
design and critically appraised the included SRs using the
AMSTAR 217 instrument. Based on this critical appraisal,
an AMSTAR 2 quality score was provided for each article
as either High, Acceptable, Low, or Unacceptable. Scoring
discrepancies were discussed between the two reviewers
and if consensus could not be reached, a third reviewer

Recommendation Development
The GDG considered the body of evidence and additional domains18,19 to guide development of the recommendations. The domains were: strength of evidence,
magnitude of effect, benefits, risks, harms, costs, value
judgments, role of patient preferences, exclusions, and
differences of opinion. Operational definitions of the
strength of recommendations based on the level of evidence and magnitude of effect are provided in Table 2. In
addition, the GDG adjusted the strength of recommendation up or down based on the benefit-harm ratio, value
judgments, and role of patient preferences. The role of
these considerations was described in the Rationale for
each recommendation.

Clinical providers and academicians with expertise in fall
risk management for older adults and CPG methodology
were invited by the GDG to review the draft guideline and
provide comments. A survey was used to elicit feedback
on key aspects, and open comment was invited. The
guideline was posted for comment for two weeks on the
APTA-Geriatrics website, and invitations were disseminated to the physical therapy community through the
Balance and Falls Special Interest Group of the Academy
of Geriatric Physical Therapy. The final recommendations
and manuscript were also reviewed by three older adult
laypersons. All comments were addressed by the GDG
and revisions and responses were documented.

required throughout the guideline development process.

Recommendation Development
The GDG considered the body of evidence and additional domains18,19 to guide development of the recommendations. The domains were: strength of evidence,
magnitude of effect, benefits, risks, harms, costs, value
judgments, role of patient preferences, exclusions, and
differences of opinion. Operational definitions of the
strength of recommendations based on the level of evidence and magnitude of effect are provided in Table 2. In
addition, the GDG adjusted the strength of recommendation up or down based on the benefit-harm ratio, value

Clinical providers and academicians with expertise in fall
risk management for older adults and CPG methodology
were invited by the GDG to review the draft guideline and
provide comments. A survey was used to elicit feedback
on key aspects, and open comment was invited. The

The results of individual systematic reviews are summarized in the accompanying tables, and the risk ratio,
rate ratio, and 95% confidence intervals are provided.
Risk ratio refers to the proportion in the number of
people falling in the intervention group compared to
a comparison group, and the rate ratio refers to the
proportion in the number of fall events in the intervention group compared to a comparison group. For both
measures, a number less than one indicates a decreased
risk and greater than 1 indicates an increased risk. The
95% confidence interval indicates the statistical significance of estimated risk or rate ratio. If the 95% confidence interval contains the value of 1.0, then the estimate
of the risk ratio or rate ratio indicates no statistically
significant difference between the control group and the
intervention group.

Screening
Physical therapists’ management of falls is predicated on
their ability to identify fall risk and movement dysfunction
as part of a multifactorial evaluation process to guide treatment choice. In 2017, through the Geriatrics Evidence
Database to Guide Effectiveness Initiative (GeriEDGE) task
force, Lusardi et al published a systematic review of history
questions, self-report measures, and performance-based
measures for assessing fall risk of community-dwelling
older adults.13 This CPG developed a screening process
using these results13 and the previous guidance statement
recommendations.12 The screening process includes medical

history questions, self-report measures, and performancebased functional measures as part of a multifactorial falls
screening13 (see Table 3). The GDG did not systematically
review the evidence for screening for falls risk, thus we
indicate the level of evidence for screening, but do not provide specific recommendations for falls risk screening.

The medical history questions, self-report measures, and
performance-based measures with the highest post-test
probability of identifying falls risk align with the Center
for Disease Control (CDC) “Stopping Elderly Accidents,
Death, and Injuries” (STEADI) processes20 and recent
guidelines on the management of falls.15 The details are
provided in the Falls Management Algorithm (Figure 1).

Screening may include self-report measures of falls selfefficacy and depression. Self-efficacy for the maintenance of
balance should be screened using the Falls Efficacy ScaleInternational,21 with scores greater than 24 indicating
increased fall risk.13 Depression is associated with impaired
mobility and increased falls incidence, and therefore screening for depression using the Geriatric Depression Scale-1522

(cut-off score >6)13 can be used to identify fall risk.

chunks.text:
Tests and measures that encompass body functions and
structures, activity and participation, and environmental
and personal factors should be performed during the
examination. Based upon positive predictive values associated with fall risk established by the GeriEDGE SR we
recommend the Timed Up and Go (TUG),23 5 times sit-tostand test,24 single limb stance with eyes open,25 the Berg
Balance Scale (BBS)26 and self-selected gait speed.27

Scores greater than 11 seconds for the TUG and/or greater
than 12 seconds on the 5 times sit-to-stand test indicate
risk for falls.13 If the older adult is unable to maintain
a single limb stance with eyes open greater than 6.5 seconds, fall risk is increased.13 A score of less than 50 on the
BBS or a Self-selected walking speed less than 1.0 m/s
indicate risk for falling.13

An intention of this CPG is to provide recommendations while considering the older adult’s level of fall risk.
Determining the level of fall risk is part of the screening
component of physical therapy management of older
adults. Providing recommendations for fall risk classification is challenging due to inconsistent definitions in the
literature, and variability in fall risk cut-off scores. As
reinforced by Lusardi et al,13 the clinician can merge the
findings of several tests to more accurately portray an
older adult’s risk of falls. The Sherrington 2019 SR28

included studies that categorized higher risk as 1 or
more falls and often some additional impairment on balance or mobility tests. The recent World CPG16 categorized high fall risk as those who had an injurious fall, 2 or
more falls, a frailty diagnosis, inability to get up from the
floor, or a loss of consciousness/suspected syncope. The
GDG considers pre-fall loss of consciousness and syncope to be separate issues and out of the scope of this
CPG. The GDG values a quantitative approach to assessing fall risk using change in post-test probability of validated questions, tests, and measures. We suggest that

those who have a history of multiple or injurious falls,
frailty, and/or are identified as having balance impairment
by evidence-based tests, as suggested by Lusardi et al,13

should be classified as high risk.

chunks.text:
Examination
After the screening process determines the level of fall risk,
physical therapy management of people at risk for falls
requires a thorough examination to identify movement
related impairments and activity limitations. The examination leads to a movement system diagnosis that enables the
development of a tailored intervention for falls management. Utilization of tests and measures with the best posttest probability for fall risk13 allows for the identification
of who is at high risk of falls, but does not identify impairments in subdomains of balance, or other specific impairments (ie, in strength, balance, or cognition) that can guide
what intervention is most appropriate for individuals.
A recent study of the BESTest and MiniBESTest may support the relevance of these tests in this population.29

Magnani et al29 suggested age-standardized cut-off points
for the BESTest and the Mini-BESTest. These tests may be
particularly relevant to this population as they allow characterization of balance during standing and walking across
multiple subdomains,29 and may better inform the evaluation and treatment planning process. Clinicians should
refer to other evidence-based guidelines to assist with
identification and classification of movement system
impairments and limitations.30-32 A systematic review of
examination strategies was outside the scope of this CPG.

MULTIFACTORIAL MANAGEMENT PROGRAMS
Multifactorial management programs include screening,
assessment, referral to appropriate provider, and interventions within physical therapist scope of practice.12

Studies of fall prevention intervention programs that
addressed multiple fall risk factors by providers from
any discipline within and outside of PT practice in which
a physical therapy provider might be involved were
included. According to the ProFaNE Taxonomy, “multifactorial interventions are those interventions in which
two or more sub-domains of intervention can be given
to participants, and the interventions are linked to
each individual’s risk profile, such that not all participants in a program receive the same combination of
sub-domains.”1

A recent study of the BESTest and MiniBESTest may support the relevance of these tests in this population.29

Magnani et al29 suggested age-standardized cut-off points
for the BESTest and the Mini-BESTest. These tests may be
particularly relevant to this population as they allow characterization of balance during standing and walking across
multiple subdomains,29 and may better inform the evaluation and treatment planning process. Clinicians should
refer to other evidence-based guidelines to assist with
identification and classification of movement system
impairments and limitations.30-32 A systematic review of
examination strategies was outside the scope of this CPG.

MULTIFACTORIAL MANAGEMENT PROGRAMS
Multifactorial management programs include screening,
assessment, referral to appropriate provider, and interventions within physical therapist scope of practice.12

Studies of fall prevention intervention programs that
addressed multiple fall risk factors by providers from
any discipline within and outside of PT practice in which
a physical therapy provider might be involved were
included. According to the ProFaNE Taxonomy, “multifactorial interventions are those interventions in which
two or more sub-domains of intervention can be given
to participants, and the interventions are linked to
each individual’s risk profile, such that not all participants in a program receive the same combination of
sub-domains.”1

provider for identified risk factors

• examination of:

º balance

º gait

º lower extremity strength

º environmental hazards

º footwear

• determined by level of fall risk, prescribing and
implementing interventions within the scope of physical therapist practice for management of falls and

º gait training

º functional training

º education

º environmental modification

Rationale
Evidence for the effectiveness of multifactorial interventions comes from eight high-quality SRs,33-40 and nine
acceptable quality SRs.41-49 Details and estimates of rate
and risk reduction can be found in Table 4. Healthy older
adults and older adults at high risk of falls receive beneficial effects from multifactorial interventions; greater
effects were seen when exercise, environmental or more
active interventions were utilized. Greater reductions in
fall rate and fall risk were found in those considered high
risk. In addition, reductions in fall rate were larger than
fall risk. Overall, the evidence supports a small-to-moderate benefit of multifactorial interventions that poses
minimal to no harm. The GDG acknowledges the need
to incorporate patient preferences in decision-making for
intervention selection, and potentially additional benefits
that extend beyond successful fall prevention (ie, reduced
fall-related injuries, fractures, mobility limitations, and
improved independence, and/or life expectancy).

Evidence Synthesis
The early literature indicated limited evidence for the
effect of multifactorial interventions and lacked precision
of the effect estimate for fall risk.43 With additional studies in 2010, the United States Preventive Services Task
Force (USPSTF)33 reported a 25% reduction in fall risk,
and concluded that there was evidence that multifactorial
interventions reduced falls among those at high risk. The
USPSTF recommendations were updated in 201850 and
2024,51 and affirmed that multifactorial interventions
should be selectively offered to older adults based on
clinicians’ findings and patients’ values and preferences.
Additional SRs built evidence for an approximately 25%
reduction of fall rate, and, in some cases, for fall risk.34,38

Larger reductions in fall rate (35-36%) were demonstrated
for interventions that included exercise, or environmental

results that were consistent with Lee et al38 including that
there was substantial heterogeneity among studies.39,40,48

Loureiro et al,49 in an acceptable quality SR, reported that
only multifactorial interventions that included exercise with
falls risk home assessment and exercise with health education showed a significant reduction in fall rate. Loureiro
et al49 also reported that when multifactorial interventions
included exercise, utilization of group exercise resulted in
reduction in fall rate, while individual exercise programs did
not have a significant effect on fall rate.

High-risk versus low-risk participants
Subgroup analyses from Gates et al43 revealed that
multifactorial interventions are effective for reducing
fall rate by 23% for people at higher risk of falls but
no effect was found in studies that did not select for
people at higher risk of falls. Meta-analysis from
Caristia et al48 showed that multifactorial interventions lasting less than 12 months were effective in
reducing falls, while those lasting more than 12 months

were not. Cheng et al46 conducted a network metaanalysis (NMA) of the comparative effectiveness of
interventions and found multifactorial intervention
compared to usual care had the greatest efficacy
(36% reduced odds) relative to several other intervention comparisons including exercise, referral, and education. However, Cheng’s definition of multifactorial
intervention resulted in inclusion of multi-component
exercise interventions that likely caused overestimation
of the effect.

EXERCISE
Physical activity can be defined as any bodily movement
produced by skeletal muscles that results in energy
expenditure.52 Exercise is a type of physical activity featuring bodily movement that is planned, structured and
repetitive and is performed with the intention of improving or maintaining physical fitness.52 In this CPG, we
focus on exercise as opposed to physical activity, as
defined above. In 2018, the USPSTF released a final
statement recommending exercise to prevent falls in
older adults based on adequate evidence,50 and reissued
the recommendation in 2024.51 This has been supported

Many high-quality SRs categorize studies using the
ProFaNE taxonomy.1 The ProFaNE taxonomy considers
the broad category of exercise by its method of delivery
and includes strength/resistance training, flexibility, general physical activity, and endurance. ProFaNE also
includes a gait, balance, and functional training category
and a category called 3D training. 3D training includes
Tai Chi, Qi Gong, and dance.1 This CPG adopts these
categories of exercise.

Systematic reviews included in this CPG calculate risk
and rate ratios by combining studies that include single
component exercise programs, multicomponent exercise
programs, or a mix of multi-component and single component exercise. The evidence from these three categories
of SRs is addressed separately. Recommendations and
descriptions of the evidence for mixed exercise (singleand multi-component) and multicomponent exercise are
provided first, followed by recommendations for each
individual exercise mode.

chunks.text:
Recommendation
Physical therapists must provide or prescribe multicomponent exercise to older adults to reduce risk and rate for
falls and it must include balance training and may include
other exercise modes. (Evidence Quality/Level: I, Rec.
Strength: Strong) Rationale
For older adults at lower risk for falls, physical therapists
must ensure participation in a multicomponent exercise regimen that includes balance exercise to manage fall risk. For
older adults with identified impairments in strength and
balance, physical therapists must provide tailored, progressive exercise to address these deficits. This strong recommendation is based on Level 1 evidence from 14 high
or moderate quality SRs of multicomponent exercise
programs,13,14,28,34,44,45,55-57,59-63 10 additional high or
moderate quality SRs of mixed single and multi-component
exercise programs,13,14,28,36,39,46,55-57,61 and 4 lower quality
SRs that did not include meta-analysis.64-67 Details and
estimates of rate and risk reduction can be found in
Table 5 for mixed multicomponent and single component
studies, and Table 6 for multicomponent studies.

risk or safety in exercising without assistance.

Multicomponent exercise programs were deemed safe,
with a large majority of studies reporting no adverse
events from participation.28,35 Overall, RCTs reported
few adverse effects after a multicomponent intervention
which included falls during exercise, pain during exercise,
muscle soreness, muscle strain, low back pain, and abnormal heart rhythm. A recent SR with meta-analysis by
Garcia-Hermoso68
examined
safety
in
RCTs
that
included long-term exercise interventions and reported
no difference between exercise and control groups in the
proportion that dropped out due to health issues or
mortality.

Evidence Synthesis
Mixed single- and multi-component exercise evidence
Systematic reviews of mixed single- and multi-component
exercise which estimate the reduction in both fall rate and
risk include one high quality39 and one acceptable quality
network meta-analysis (NMA).46 The high-quality study
found an 8% reduction in fall risk and a 10% reduction in
fall rate, while the acceptable quality study found a 33%
reduction in fall risk. It is not clear if the discrepancy in
fall risk is due to quality or that the high-quality study was
limited to studies with falls as a primary outcome.

Systematic reviews with meta-analyses which estimate
the reduction in fall rate and risk included four high
quality14,28,35,55 and five acceptable quality13,54-56,58

studies. The nine meta-analyses13,14,28,35,54-58 showed
a reduction in fall rate (13% to 32%), and fall risk
(11% to 22%). Two of these meta-analyses had unique
inclusion criteria and fall outcomes.55,58 El Khoury et al55

included only injurious falls and found a 37% reduction
in fall rate. Wong58 only included studies with fall and
fracture rates and found a 29% reduction in falls and
a 46% reduction in fractures.

Multicomponent exercise evidence
Multicomponent exercise to reduce fall rate and fall risk is
supported by 14 meta-analyses.13,14,28,34,38,44,48,54,56,59-63

Multicomponent exercise resulted in a reduction in fall rate
(21-28%) and risk (22-27%).14,28,34 Caristia et al48 only
included studies that enrolled participants who were not
considered frail and found a higher (31%) reduction in fall
rate. In another high-quality SR with meta-analysis, Lee
et al38 examined studies that included multicomponent
exercise as part of a multifactorial program and found
a 34% reduction in falls rate and 21% reduction in fall
risk. Thus SRs with different methodologies and inclusion
criteria show similar rate and risk reductions, supporting
this strong recommendation.

Mixed single- and multi-component exercise evidence
Systematic reviews of mixed single- and multi-component
exercise which estimate the reduction in both fall rate and
risk include one high quality39 and one acceptable quality
network meta-analysis (NMA).46 The high-quality study
found an 8% reduction in fall risk and a 10% reduction in
fall rate, while the acceptable quality study found a 33%
reduction in fall risk. It is not clear if the discrepancy in
fall risk is due to quality or that the high-quality study was
limited to studies with falls as a primary outcome.

Systematic reviews with meta-analyses which estimate
the reduction in fall rate and risk included four high
quality14,28,35,55 and five acceptable quality13,54-56,58

studies. The nine meta-analyses13,14,28,35,54-58 showed
a reduction in fall rate (13% to 32%), and fall risk
(11% to 22%). Two of these meta-analyses had unique
inclusion criteria and fall outcomes.55,58 El Khoury et al55

included only injurious falls and found a 37% reduction
in fall rate. Wong58 only included studies with fall and
fracture rates and found a 29% reduction in falls and
a 46% reduction in fractures.

Multicomponent exercise to reduce fall rate and fall risk is
supported by 14 meta-analyses.13,14,28,34,38,44,48,54,56,59-63

Multicomponent exercise resulted in a reduction in fall rate
(21-28%) and risk (22-27%).14,28,34 Caristia et al48 only
included studies that enrolled participants who were not
considered frail and found a higher (31%) reduction in fall
rate. In another high-quality SR with meta-analysis, Lee
et al38 examined studies that included multicomponent
exercise as part of a multifactorial program and found
a 34% reduction in falls rate and 21% reduction in fall

Recent SRs by Papalia et al,62 Wong et al,58 and
Hamed et al57 performed meta-analyses in which most
of the studies were included in previous SRs. The results of
the analyses were consistent with other SRs and most of
the RCTs included multicomponent exercise but these
analyses did not break down the types of exercise as we
do in this CPG.58,62 Hamed et al57 included only RCTs
with longer follow-up periods, and found a slightly higher
reduction in fall rate (32%) and risk (22%), suggesting
that the positive benefit of exercise programs can be longlasting.

Many SRs examining multicomponent programs
include studies in which the Otago exercise program was
the intervention. The Otago exercise program is a homebased exercise program that includes balance exercises,
resistance training, and a walking program.59 One moderate quality SR with meta-analysis59 compared the
Otago exercise program to no treatment control or social
visits and found a 14% reduction in fall risk. One SR
without meta-analysis examined the effectiveness of functional exercise like the Lifestyle Integrated Functional
Exercise (LIFE) program and found 31% reduction in
fall rates in two studies.67

Group vs. individual
More studies of multicomponent exercise involved group
rather than individual interventions.28,34 Individual interventions are delivered in one-on-one clinical settings, and
individualized exercise is tailored to the specific problems
identified by a physical therapy examination. Although
reported inconsistently in the literature, group exercise
is presumed to be not tailored to the individual, while

individual exercise may or may not be individualized or
tailored to specific individuals. We found no direct comparisons between group and individual exercise in the
same population, however several SRs included separate
sub-analyses of group programs and individual programs.

Gillespie et al,34 found no difference between group or
individual delivery of multicomponent exercise for fall
rate (29% vs 32% reduction) or risk (15% vs 22% reduction) as evidenced by overlapping confidence intervals. In
a more recent high-quality SR, Sherrington et al14 found
no difference between group and individual exercise programs for fall rate, with 26% risk reduction in group
settings and 19% risk reduction in individual settings. In
another moderate quality SR with meta-analysis investigating group plus home-based exercise programs in people with identified risk factors for falls, Teng et al63 found
no reduction in fall risk. Therefore, we are unable to make
a recommendation about group vs individual exercise,
thus the patient preference, availability and cost may
guide the decision about the best delivery mode to reduce
falls.

chunks.text:
Delivery personnel
In two high-quality SRs, Sherrington compared multicomponent interventions that were delivered by health
care professionals versus non-health care professionals,
and found no difference in fall rate or fall risk between
delivery by health care professionals and by non-health
care professionals.14,28 One low-quality SR without metaanalysis66 found that most physical therapist-led group
exercise programs reduced fall rates, but not more than
individualized physical therapy programs. These results
should be interpreted with caution as it is unclear if the
samples in these studies were similar enough to make
a direct comparison or were generalizable to a wider
population. For example, older adults who participate in
a community-based program delivered by a non-health
care professional might have less frailty or more ability
to exercise independently than those who participate in
programs delivered by a physical therapist or other health
care professional.

High-risk vs low-risk older adults
The evidence on the effect of multicomponent exercise on
older adults identified as being at a higher risk vs lower
risk of falling does not allow for separate recommendations. Gillespie et al34 found a similar reduction in fall rate
in studies that selected for people at high risk of falls and
in studies that did not (30% vs 28% rate reduction).
Sherrington et al14 also reported no differences between
studies that recruited older adults selected for high risk
and those that did not (24% vs 22% rate reduction,
respectively). In contrast, in one moderate-quality SR
that examined home-based individualized exercise programs, there was no effect on fall risk when including
studies of people who were recently discharged from the

hospital, but a 16% risk reduction when those studies
were excluded.61 Because this moderate quality study is
focused on home therapy alone, the GDG does not believe
that this study provides enough evidence of a differential
effect between people at higher and lower risk.

Two SRs with meta-analysis44,60 found large reductions in the fall rate and risk when including only studies
that recruited individuals with health conditions that
might impact falls. Liu et al,60 in a moderate quality
review that included only people with reduced physical
capacity, found a 37% reduction in fall rate, and Petridou
et al44 found an even larger 55% reduction in the fall risk
when examining studies that included only people with
a history of falls. Thus, we are unable to make separate
recommendations about high-risk individuals vs the general population and recommend that physical therapists
use clinical judgment based on individual patient examination of the movement system, patient safety, and
patient preferences.

Recommendation: Dosage, Intensity, and Components
Physical therapists must prescribe exercise programs to
older adults to be performed at least 150 minutes to
3 hours per week, lasting from 6 to 12 months, and
must include progressive and sufficiently challenging
balance training. (Evidence Quality/Level: I, Strength:
Strong)

Rationale
Multicomponent exercise programs that include more
than 150 minutes of exercise weekly are most effective
in reducing fall rates48 and programs of 6 to 12 months
duration are most effective in reducing fall rate and risk.60

Evidence from one meta-analysis61 examining the most
effective combination of exercises in studies with longer
follow-up times indicated that the most effective combination reduced risk by 35%, and included all categories of
exercise combined, including gait, balance, and functional
training, resistance training, flexibility exercises, and 3D
training such as Tai Chi or dance.

Evidence Synthesis
Duration, intensity, and components of mixed singleand multi-component exercise programs
In three separate SRs, Sherrington et al13,14,54 investigated
the intensity, duration, and components of mixed singleand multi-component exercise interventions and found
that the highest rate reductions were found with programs
that included high intensity/high challenge balance training, did not include walking programs, had doses greater
than 50 hours, and had frequencies greater than 3 hours
per week. Differences in fall risk and rate reduction
according to duration, intensity, or exercise components
are summarized in Table 7. The most recent high-quality
SR14 showed a 50% reduction in falls in programs that
included more than 3 hours per week and balance and
functional training.

chunks.text:
Duration, intensity and components of
multicomponent exercise programs
Evidence from a moderate quality SR with meta-analysis
by Caristia et al48 demonstrated that exercise programs at
an intensity of more than 150 minutes weekly decreased
falls by 47% in contrast to a 12% decrease in fall rate in
studies that had intensities less than 150 minutes weekly.
Another SR with meta-analysis56 provides level I evidence
of higher reductions in risk (36%) and rate (33%) in
studies lasting between 6 and 12 months than studies
less than 12 months or more than 12 months. Estimates
of risk and rate ratios by intensity and duration of

intervention from SRs of multicomponent interventions
are found in Table 8.

BALANCE TRAINING
Balance training is included in the Gait, Balance,
Functional Training delivery mode of exercise in the
ProFaNE taxonomy.1 Systematic reviews categorized balance training using different terminology: by the ProFaNE
category, by balance training generally, or by several
explicit methods such as volitional or reactive step training,
or gait adaptability training. While the ProFaNE definition
of balance is compatible with those used in physical therapy, this CPG considers a conceptual framework that
includes steady state (controlling the location of the
body’s center of mass within the area defined by the base
of support under predictable, quasi-static conditions),30

anticipatory (generating postural adjustments prior to or
during voluntary movement to counter an upcoming postural disturbance or realigning the body’s center of mass),30

and reactive (responding to sensory input that signals
a need for a response to ensure successful maintenance
of postural control.)30 postural control strategies as
a foundation to examine balance dysfunction and to target
balance exercises accordingly.30 Therefore, balance training, such as volitional and reactive step training, when
individualized to the patient, will specifically target
impaired postural control processes.

chunks.text:
Balance training must include volitional step training
and/or gait adaptability training (Evidence quality/level: I,
Recommendation strength: Strong).

Balance training may also include reactive step (perturbation) training (Evidence quality/level II, Recommendation
strength: Weak).

Rationale
The recommendation is based on six high-quality SRs with
meta-analyses14,28,34,69-71 and three acceptable quality
SRs.56,72,73 The strength of this recommendation is based
on the preponderance of benefit via consistent reductions
in fall rate and risk across multiple high-quality SRs with
balance as an element of a multicomponent exercise program, and moderate to large benefit when provided alone.

Evidence for the benefit of balance training to reduce
fall rates and risk is supported by many SRs and guidance
statements. Gillespie et al34 demonstrated a 28% reduction in fall rate and 19% reduction in fall risk. Similar rate
and risk reductions have been confirmed for balance
training by Sherrington et al29 with 24% and 13% reductions, respectively. Estimates of risk and rate reduction
from gait, balance and functional training programs can
be found in Table 10. Earlier expert recommendations
advocated for a progressive and challenging nature to
balance training.14 This means that task and environmental manipulations must be employed throughout the training program. For example, upper limb support should be
reduced over time. The base of support should be reduced
to provide challenges to balance when standing or walking. Finally, limb and body movements should occur
under voluntary and reactive conditions.

Recent studies have provided additional clarity on the
nature and form of training required to produce benefit.69-71

The progressive and challenging nature of balance training
remains critical for fall rate and risk reductions. For example, movements requiring changes to the base of support
should include voluntary stepping that is self-directed or
verbally or visually cued and executed in multiple directions
(eg, forward, backward, laterally). Most studies examining
volitional step training provide stepping targets under varied
cognitive conditions, square-stepping, and/or exergaming
step training. Movements that require changes to the
base of support can also be reactive in nature. Reactive
step training refers to individualized interventions
which include external perturbations while standing
still or walking overground, on a treadmill, or in a
virtual environment, and usually occurring in a clinical
environment. Some studies examining reactive step
training provide perturbations through complex technology which adds cost and staff training time. Both
volitional and reactive step training produce reductions
in fall risk and rate.69,70

quality of evidence for perturbation training, and
the uncertainty of type of perturbation (belt, walkway,
treadmill) on community falls compared to laboratory

falls,71,74 further research is warranted to examine perturbation training within the clinical setting using relatively less-expensive equipment to determine if the form of
perturbation training has a differential effect on fall risk
and rate. Furthermore, it is uncertain currently who benefits the most and if reactive step training employing
external perturbations is superior to multicomponent
exercise or volitional step training.

Similar to step training, gait adaptability training provides opportunities for employing proactive and reactive
postural control strategies during ambulation. Norgaard
et al71 defined gait adaptability training as making quick
and appropriate modifications to walking in response to
environmental challenges such as avoiding or accommodating obstacles or stepping to specific targets. This can be
done during overground walking or in a virtual environment. Similar risks exist during gait adaptability training
compared to step training in standing. The benefits of gait
adaptability training include reductions in fall risk and
rate. It is unclear currently if gait adaptability training
alone is superior to multicomponent exercise.

Step and gait adaptability training should be individualized, challenging, and progressive. To be individualized,
the physical therapist should address the impact of the
underlying determinants of postural control. For example, if fear is a factor, then progression should be incremental using improved balance confidence as a guide to
increase challenges to balance. If use of sensory information is a factor, then conducting step training under varied
and altered sensory conditions is warranted. Challenges
to balance during step training occur through modifying
the task or environmental configuration and context.
Commonly manipulated task and environmental conditions during step training include sensory conditions such
as reducing or eliminating vision, support surface compliance, and the use of concurrent cognitive and/or focal
motor tasks. Direction of perturbation (anterior/posterior, lateral) should be considered along with task context
(standing, walking) and individualized to the patient’s
needs.

Given the ecological validity and potential carryover to
real world settings, the GDG placed high value on incorporating gait adaptability training as part of a multicomponent exercise program. We also placed value on step
training (volitional and reactive) as it requires a change in
the patient’s base of support through engaging proactive
(volitional) or reactive (through external perturbation)
postural control mechanisms.

chunks.text:
Evidence Synthesis
Norgaard et al71 evaluated 11 studies in an SR with metaanalysis and found gait adaptability training resulted in
a 42% reduction in fall rate with moderate certainty.
They also found the proportion of fall-related fractures
and fall risk was reduced by 81% and 43%, respectively,
however, with low or very low certainty because the
analysis was based on only two studies and a small

number of fall events. The type of gait adaptability training interventions included stepping during virtual reality
exercise games, treadmill walking with virtual reality,
volitional, multi-targeted, and square stepping training,
obstacle course navigation, and multitask and interactive
cognitive-motor stepping games. Therefore, as defined,
gait adaptability training shares many features of volitional step training with the added application of navigating open, challenging environments.

Dennett and Taylor72 compared exergaming interventionstotraditionalinterventionsin anSRwith meta-analysis.
Only one analysis on fall risk using three studies comparing
exergaming with a balance focus against traditional balance
training applied to this CPG. Results were determined to be
non-significant, and two of the studies were very low quality.

Okubo et al conducted a meta-analysis69 with low risk
of bias including seven studies of volitional and reactive
step training in older persons not selected for the level of
fall risk. Overall, step training reduced the rate of falls by
52% and the risk for falls by 49%. Three studies were
used to examine the effects of volitional step training on
risk and rate of falls. Volitional step training reduced the
risk of falls by 58% and the rate of falls by 57%. Four
studies were used to examine the effects of reactive step
training on fall risk and rate. Reactive step training
reduced fall risk by 40% and fall rate by 48%.

Papadimitriou et al70 conducted a meta-analysis of
studies examining the effects of perturbation training in
community-dwelling older persons at increased risk for
falling. When perturbation training was added to standard physical therapy and compared to a multimodal
exercise program including strengthening, flexibility,
and dynamic balance exercises (one study, 64 older
adults), the intervention had an uncertain effect on fall
risk. When perturbation training as a stand-alone intervention was compared to a single slip perturbation, volitional step training, no training, or flexibility and
relaxation exercises, perturbation training showed an
uncertain effect on fall risk. Studies in this meta-analysis
were determined to be low-quality and exhibiting a high
risk of bias.70

chunks.text:
Mansfield et al73 conducted an SR with meta-analysis
of eight studies that included some form of perturbation
training with results favoring the intervention. However,
three studies included people with Parkinson’s disease.
Therefore, we were unable to use the meta-analysis results
in this CPG. Of note, Papadimitriou et al70 reactive step
training analysis included 3 of the 4 studies included in
Mansfield.73

Some SRs did not provide details on the nature and
form of balance training, as compared to SRs that were
explicitly descriptive or were described as step training or
gait adaptability training. For example, Sherrington
201928 and 202014 categorized balance training within
the ProFaNE definition of gait, balance, and functional
training.1 When the broad category of balance and functional exercise was considered, Sherrington et al14,28

found fall risk was reduced by 13% and fall rate was
reduced by 24%.

Group vs individual
In one high-quality SR, Sherrington et al28 analyzed balance and functional training delivered in group and individual settings. Results were nearly identical for either
delivery method, with 27% falls rate reduction with
group exercise compared to 23% falls rate reduction
with individual exercise. Both group and individual exercise showed a 13% reduction in fall risk. The GDG found
no direct comparison between group and individual exercise in the literature.

Delivery personnel
In one high-quality SR, Sherrington28 analyzed balance
and functional training delivered by health care professionals and non-health care professionals. There was
a slightly greater effect on fall risk and rate when balance
training was delivered by health care professionals (18%
vs 11% fall risk reduction and 33 vs 18% fall rate
reduction).

High-risk vs low-risk subjects
The evidence about the effect of general balance and
functional training on older adults identified as being at
a higher risk of falling is inconclusive with a similar reduction in fall risk (12% reduction when not selected for
higher risk vs 14% fall risk reduction when selected for
higher risk) and a slightly higher fall rate reduction when
selected for higher risk (28 vs 20%).28

RESISTANCE TRAINING
This section includes studies that provided resistance
exercise as a sole intervention for fall risk reduction.
Resistance exercise includes all components of muscle
power and strength training, contracting the muscles
against resistance to overload the body sufficiently to
bring about a training effect. This may include increasing
external force by changing a position (ie, gravity-based
functional resistance exercises) or using an external
resistance.1 The evidence to support resistance exercise
comes from SRs and meta-analyses that report the effect
on fall risk and/or fall rate.

chunks.text:
effectiveness of balance training to reduce fall risk, providing resistance training ALONE is not sufficient. For
people with identified impairments, it is the standard of
practice to provide tailored, progressive resistance exercises to address these deficits within a multicomponent
plan.

Resistance exercise ALONE was not recommended due
to the uncertainty of its effect on fall rate and risk. The
studies that we reviewed had several limitations such as
small sample sizes, no study stratified by their sample by
risk of falls, and moderate-to-high risk of bias was present.
The overwhelming majority of studies reported minimal
adverse events from resistance training performed as part
of a multicomponent exercise program, such as falls during
exercise, pain during exercise, muscle soreness, muscle
strain, low back pain, and abnormal heart rhythm.

Evidence Synthesis
Overall, the rate ratios are of low clinically meaningful
value with insignificant confidence intervals. Estimates
of risk and rate ratios are found in Table 11. Metaanalysis of acceptable or higher quality that found resistance training alone reported >1.0 fall rate ratio in two
studies,14,28 no change in rate ratio in a study,75 and
reduced rate ratio in one study.48 Fall risk ratio had
similar findings with three of three studies reporting
a ratio between 0.81 and 1.00 with insignificant confidence intervals.28,75,76 In one SR without metaanalysis,77 resistance training was viewed favorably
concerning fall risk reduction when applied conventionally or as part of ADLs and when compared to usual care
or relaxation training.

Resistance training protocols employed differing doses
and formats. Individual studies from the meta-analyses
were further explored to identify specific characteristics
for frequency, intensity, time, and types. Resistance exercise
was often group-based, performed for 50-minute sessions,
two-to-three times per week for 25 to 52 weeks.78-80 None
of the studies demonstrated a decrease in fall rate or risk.
The lack of change supports the recommendation that
resistance training should not be performed in isolation,
but as a component of a patient management plan as recommended in the multicomponent recommendation section.

The safety of resistance training was further demonstrated in a recent meta-analysis of RCTs of long-term
exercise interventions that found no difference between
exercise and control groups in dropout due to health
issues or mortality.68

chunks.text:
Limitations in study design and reporting limit the
ability to fully elucidate the importance of resistance
training for falls. No studies were stratified by risk of
falls, bias risk was consistently moderate-to-high, studies
were limited by relatively small sample sizes, and resistance
exercise was not commonly separated from multicomponent exercise protocols. Multicomponent protocols found
no effect on fall rate when either moderate or high-intensity
resistance training was included.54 Multimodal exercise
that included resistance training was analyzed in a recent
meta-analysis of RCT and found no effect on fall rate or
fall risk.76

The multicomponent or multimodal design of RCTs
and subsequent meta-analyses limits the ability to distinguish the impact of resistance training alone. A systematic
investigation with meta-analysis of the effectiveness of
resistance training as a single modality or part of a multimodal program in reducing fall rate or fall risk would
support recommendations in this area. Furthermore, the
effectiveness of unsupervised home-based resistance training programs in reducing falls has not been confirmed by
existing SRs.75

TAI CHI
In this CPG, Tai Chi refers to any form of Chinese martial
art consisting of a series of slow, low-impact, bodily
movements. One form, Yang-style, includes 24 different
forms that incorporate multidirectional weight shifting,
awareness of body alignment, and multisegmental movement coordination. Tai Chi is often included as a 3D
exercise in the ProFaNE taxonomy.1 The evidence comes
from SRs and meta-analyses that report the effect of Tai
Chi on fall risk and fall rate.

chunks.text:
Tai Chi is most often delivered in a group setting and
by trained instructors such as a Tai Chi practitioner.
Physical therapists can provide Tai Chi if they are trained
instructors.

We placed a high value on the group exercise nature of
Tai Chi. Most included studies used a version of Yangstyle Tai Chi. One SR determined Yang style may have
a greater effect on fall risk and rate than Sun style.81

However, the analysis for Sun style was based on only
three studies and this analysis may be influenced by publication bias. Therefore, we did not provide a recommendation on the style of Tai Chi to be used.

While there are benefits for older adults participating
in community-based Tai Chi intervention programs,
availability, and cost of programming along with patient
preference related to the type of exercise should be considered. Older persons may inquire about and physical
therapists should inform older adults of intervention
options if there are Tai Chi programs in their geographic
vicinity.

The GDG placed value on Tai Chi as an effective intervention for reducing fall rate and fall risk in older adults, in
particular, the GDG valued Tai Chi as an intervention for
those at lower risk of falling. Due to evidence variability,
the GDG intentionally refrained from prescribing specific
dosing and Tai Chi style recommendations. Patient preferences were recognized as crucial, considering factors such
as program availability and cost.

Evidence Synthesis
Tai Chi resulted in a 29% to 48% reduction in fall rate
and a 20% to 43% reduction in fall risk. Risk and rate
ratios varied according to the type of Tai Chi, fall risk
status of the participants, time of follow-up, and type of
control group. Estimates of fall risk and rate reduction for
studies that included Tai Chi or dance are found in
Table 12.

Higher vs lower risk of falls
There is an abundance of evidence that the magnitude of
effect is greater for persons designated as lower risk of
falling, nevertheless, persons at higher risk may benefit
from Tai Chi. The definitions of higher and lower risk of
falling varied among SRs and no standard definition could
be ascertained from the evidence.

Tai Chi is an effective intervention strategy for reducing rates of falls and fall risk in older persons living in the
community who are high functioning or have a lower fall
risk. In studies in which participants were not stratified or

selected according to risk level, fall rate reductions ranged
from 19% to 49%. Similarly, fall risk reductions ranged
from 20% to 42%. Specifically, Sherrington et al14 demonstrated a 19% rate reduction and Gillespie et al34 reported
a 41% rate reduction while Logghe et al84 reported a 49%
average reduction in fall rate.

The overall reduction in falls from Tai Chi is less in
those who were considered at high risk for falling. Huang
et al81 found a 10% reduction in fall risk and 17% fall
rate reduction when individuals were selected for higher
risk. This is compared to a 38% and 22% reduction in fall
risk and rate, respectively, for persons at lower fall risk.
Lomas-Vega et al82 included higher-risk older adults and
included all studies from a previous meta-analysis of Tai
Chi34 and demonstrated a 43% reduction in falls over the
short time (less than 12 months) and a 13% reduction in
fall rate over the long-term (greater than or equal to
12 months).82 The included RCTs did not report any
serious adverse events with Tai Chi practice. No effect
of Tai Chi on time to first fall was found. For persons at
higher risk of falling, the magnitude of the effect is greater
when also participating in multicomponent exercise than
for Tai Chi alone (refer to multicomponent exercise in
Table 6). Therefore, we recommend that multicomponent
exercise be the first choice of treatment over Tai Chi alone
when persons are at high risk of falling.

Finally, the combined insights from multiple SRs without meta-analysis investigating Tai Chi’s effectiveness in
fall prevention among older adults reveal a nuanced landscape. Reviews by Low et al85 and Liu et al86 showed
mixed results, with some studies and analyses showing
a reduction in fall risk and rate, while others failing to
demonstrate risk reduction. For example, one intervention trial showed risk reduction in the whole group and
the pre-frail older adults, but an increased risk in those
who were classified as frail.87 The SR by Liu et al,86 also
showed fall rates decreasing in some but not all studies
reviewed, and that fear of falling was more consistently
reduced than falls rate.86 Gregory and Watson88 and
Leung et al89 highlighted Tai Chi’s positive impact on
healthy older individuals but not frail older participants.
Harling et al90 indicated limited evidence for fall reduction, especially in non-high-risk groups. Overall, this evidence is influenced by factors like study quality and
participant characteristics.

Evidence on the effects of duration and intensity for Tai Chi
is emerging. Estimates of rate and risk reduction according
to intensity and duration of Tai Chi interventions is summarized in Table 13. Interventions ranged from 1 to 3 or
more times per week, typically performed for 60 minutes
for 5 to 12 months. Huang et al81 analyzed the impact of
dosage and frequency on fall risk and rate, reporting that
30 to 60 total hours of Tai Chi produced the greatest

The overall reduction in falls from Tai Chi is less in

risk. This is compared to a 38% and 22% reduction in fall
risk and rate, respectively, for persons at lower fall risk.
Lomas-Vega et al82 included higher-risk older adults and
included all studies from a previous meta-analysis of Tai
Chi34 and demonstrated a 43% reduction in falls over the
short time (less than 12 months) and a 13% reduction in
fall rate over the long-term (greater than or equal to
12 months).82 The included RCTs did not report any
serious adverse events with Tai Chi practice. No effect
of Tai Chi on time to first fall was found. For persons at
higher risk of falling, the magnitude of the effect is greater
when also participating in multicomponent exercise than
for Tai Chi alone (refer to multicomponent exercise in
Table 6). Therefore, we recommend that multicomponent
exercise be the first choice of treatment over Tai Chi alone
when persons are at high risk of falling.

Rationale
Evidence from one high-quality SR34 and one NMA46 indicates that education alone does not reduce the fall rate or
risk. Benefits of tailored education in addition to exercise
intervention may include increased knowledge and adherence to exercise and fall risk reduction management plans.
Educational materials should consider the learning style
and literacy of the patient or client. Although individualized
patient education is presumed to be the standard of care for
all older adults, it must not be used as the sole intervention.

Evidence Synthesis
Estimates of risk and rate reduction in studies including
educational intervention are summarized in Table 14.

chunks.text:
falling.92 Another large high-quality SR found that in
studies where individuals were not selected for high
risk there was no risk or rate reduction with environmental assessment and modification, but studies that
selected for high risk subjects had a 48% reduction in
falls and a 15% reduction in fall risk.34 Similarly,
Dautzenberg et al39 found no effect for environmental
modification in reducing fall risk in the general community-dwelling population, but found a 15% risk reduction in people over 75 years of age.

Environmental assessment and modification as part of
multifactorial intervention
Finally, Lee et al38 (2020) conducted a high-quality SR
with meta-analysis and found that multifactorial interventions that did not incorporate environmental assessment
and modification had no effect on fall risk or fall rate.
Multifactorial interventions that included environmental

assessment and reduced fall rates by 35% and fall risk
by 20%.

Dissemination Plans
The primary purpose of the CPG is to provide guidance
for physical therapy management of falls and fall risk
based on a comprehensive review and synthesis of the
best-available evidence. Publication of this CPG will be
announced via press release by APTA-Geriatrics, and disseminated via online resources, social media, pocket
guides, and continuing education courses at professional
conferences. The knowledge translation task force of
APTA-Geriatrics will facilitate the creation of additional
implementation tools during the three years following the
publication of this CPG.

Revision Plan
This CPG will be subject to an evidence surveillance process periodically within the first five years. Criteria for
revision, reaffirmation, or withdrawal include changes in
evidence on the benefit and harms of any of the interventions in this CPG, changes in available interventions, and
current practice patterns including validity of existing
screening and assessment procedures and tests for fall
prediction.20,93 APTA-Geriatrics leadership will determine a revision coordinator to assist in this process.

The authors would like to acknowledge the contributions

Blunt and Pamela Bagley, and University of Pittsburgh
librarian Rose Turner for their guidance and assistance

Nina Kelly, PT, DPT, and Alex Nguyen, PT, DPT assisted
with article procurement.

reviewers: Jason Falvey, PhD, DPT, University of
Maryland, Allon Goldberg, PhD, PT, University of

Arkansas.

attention to truth and detail in providing evidence to
guide physical therapist practice inspired us throughout
the completion of this work.
